items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: And he asked me when I was gonna pay him his money and I said as soon as I start making some money, and he said, okay.

ctx.x: And we were buddies. But I went in and I sat in with Giuffre for Dupree, and Giuffre Dupree wanted me to open up with him down at the Vanguard, and I didn't tell you this story, but back in the late fifties, '59, I hung strung out there in Harlem, and I come over to Brooklyn, and I had all my clothes and what not in this pawn shop, and I was going over there to get -- the guy knew me and all, I needed a few dollars, and I said, "Come on man, add some more on to the ticket, you know, and I'll come and get my…

get around, and that person wouldn't kill me until they got their fiddle, you know. It turned out later that it was Peck Morrison's bass. But however, naturally, we had to report it to the police, and that's when they started looking for me. That was before I went to Chicago, and I'm not thinking about that so much, because I knew he got his fiddle the next day; he got it back, but the police was still looking for me for petit petty larceny. And it didn't come to the floor until I got back there in '60, and I…

And, at that particular time, Frank Sinatra, as well as Sophie Tucker refused to work in New York in those big rooms unless they abolished that cabaret card business. And that made the police department mad, and they started going around raiding the clubs, and whoever had any kind of minor bust, you know, they were snatching their cards from them.
